news.Title: Is Constellation Stock a Buy After Jumping 12% on Google's 20-Year Nuclear Deal?
news.Content:
Shares of Constellation Energy (NASDAQ: CEG) jumped from $291.11 on Oct. 6 to $309.80 the same day following the announcement of its landmark 20-year power purchase agreement (PPA) and strategic collaboration with Alphabet .

There was plenty of enthusiasm for the $4.3 billion deal, which will add 890 megawatts of new nuclear capacity through updates at 11 Constellation-owned nuclear units in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, in the days since the announcement, Consellation stock is actually down more than 3%. The reason is that the energy stock is already trading at a high multiple relative to its peers, at more than 28 times trailing earnings and more than 23 times forward earnings.

Here are three reasons why Constellation is worth that lofty valuation after the Alphabet agreement.

The deal provides cash flow security

The deal locks in long-term demand over a 15- to 20-year horizon. It also has an additional 15-year agreement covering 2,700 megawatts from Constellation's existing nuclear fleet. Pairing the Alphabet announcement with a similar recent $3 billion, 20-year deal with Amazon establishes a predictable baseline of contracted cash flows.

This shields a significant portion of Constellation's nuclear fleet from merchant power price volatility and guarantees high-margin monetization for decades.

Instead of worrying about the typical construction delays, budget overruns, and regulatory hurdles connected with building nuclear plants from scratch, this deal focuses on uprates, which increase the maximum licensed electricity output of an existing, operational nuclear reactor. These include modernizing turbines, steam generators, and controls at existing facilities.

Just look at what happened with the last two new reactors, Georgia Power's Vogtle 3 and Vogtle 4 plants in Georgia, which cost more than $35 billion to build and took 15 years to build. Constellation is updating reactors already in place, a far more economical process, and expects to have the updates ready in 2028.

Analysts have an average price target of $341.53 for the stock, well above its current trading price.

Constellation isn't really overpriced

The stock is trading at lower valuations than its historical averages. That's because its shares have fallen more than 17% so far this year. It isn't fair to compare Constellation to other nuclear power stocks, as there isn't a direct comparison. Constellation operates the largest nuclear fleet in the U.S., about one-fifth of all nuclear capacity in this country.

Story Continues

Through six months, the company reported revenue of $18.6 billion, up 44.5%, year over year. Earnings per share were $5.88, an increase of 92.7% over the same six months a year ago. Those numbers show that the mystery isn't the company's valuation, but why it isn't even higher.

The company is a go-to for hyperscalers

Its size and scope mean Constellation is best positioned to benefit from the growing need for stable power for data centers, as it can provide 22 gigawatts of carbon-free nuclear power, three times more than any other utility in the U.S.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet require firm, 24/7 carbon-free power to fuel energy-hungry artificial intelligence data centers, making intermittent renewables insufficient on their own. This deal, alongside consecutive mega-deals from other tech giants, validates that nuclear operators possess irreplaceable pricing power. It also shows that tech companies are willing to heavily co-invest to secure reliable electricity.

Most of Constellation's nuclear assets are on the PJM Interconnection grid. PJM encompasses Northern Virginia and the surrounding Mid-Atlantic regions, with the highest density of data center infrastructure in the world.

Individual hyperscalers are asking for multi-gigawatt commitments. Constellation is one of the only energy providers in the country with a large enough portfolio to handle multiple GW-scale agreements without exhausting its asset base.

Worth it, despite some risks

There are legitimate reasons that Constellation isn't trading higher. It's important to note that revenue from these uprates won't begin until 2028, leaving the stock vulnerable to a broader tech sector sell-off, especially if artificial intelligence (AI) spending cools.

However, these deals also de-risk the company's investments in expanding its nuclear capacity. Constellation shouldn't be viewed as another boring utility stock but as a prime enabler of infrastructure for AI data centers. It expects more than 20% EPS growth through 2029, and based on its first-half earnings, is delivering on that forecast.

news.Title: Microsoft (MSFT) Built a $100B Azure. Can It Outrun Its Own Spending?
news.Content:
When Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) reports again later this month, one line will draw more attention than the rest: how fast Azure grew. That's a lot of weight for a single business inside a company that also sells Windows, Office, Xbox, and LinkedIn. But Azure has earned the spotlight.

Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform. Businesses rent its computing power, storage, and AI tools to run their own apps and models. They pay as they use it, so every new AI workload becomes recurring revenue. In fiscal 2026, Azure's revenue passed $100 billion for the first time, according to CEO Satya Nadella, a milestone that cements Microsoft's standing among the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires . The catch is what it costs to keep that engine growing. Whether the stock looks fairly priced comes down to one thing: can Azure's growth keep outrunning the bill?

Customers Have Already Signed Up

Azure revenue jumped 43% in fiscal Q4 2026, the most recent quarter on the books. That helped lift the Intelligent Cloud segment to $39.3 billion, up 32%.

Speed is only half the story, though. The stronger evidence of a moat sits in commercial remaining performance obligation (contracted revenue not yet recognized), which climbed 84% to $678 billion. Enterprise customers don't sign commitments that size with a provider they plan to leave, a massive backlog that cements Microsoft's top ranking on lists like the 10 Best Cloud Computing Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires .

Microsoft's other advantage is distribution. Companies already living in Microsoft 365 are an easy sell for AI add-ons, and Microsoft 365 Copilot has topped 30 million paid seats, per Nadella. The broader Microsoft Cloud business brought in $59.3 billion in the quarter, up 27%.

Profits Kept Pace

Fast growth doesn't mean much if margins buckle under it. In fiscal Q4, revenue and operating income both rose 18%, a sign the cloud boom isn't being bought with thinner profits yet. Earnings need one clarification. GAAP diluted EPS came in at $4.81, but that figure was lifted by net gains tied to Microsoft's OpenAI stake. Non-GAAP EPS of $4.74, up 23%, strips those out, so it's the cleaner read on the operating business. For the full fiscal year, non-GAAP EPS reached $17.28, up 22%. Not everything is humming. More Personal Computing revenue slipped 4%, with Xbox content and services down 10%. That just underlines how much of the story now rests on the cloud.

Is Microsoft Spending Too Much to Stay Ahead?

This is the worry that won't go away, and if you own the stock, it's the one worth watching. Capital expenditures hit $35.8 billion in fiscal Q4, against $17.1 billion a year earlier. For the full year, spending reached $115.9 billion, up from $64.6 billion.

Story Continues

Those data centers and chips will show up as depreciation for years, whether or not demand holds. If Azure growth cools while the spending keeps climbing, margins are where the pain would show first, a key risk that investors must weigh across the Top 10 AI Stocks That Will Skyrocket .

The counterweight is that $678 billion order book. Microsoft isn't building on hope alone; much of the demand it's building for is already under contract. That doesn't erase the risk, but it shrinks it.

Cheaper Than Its Own History

At a forward P/E of 27.39, as of October 12, investors are paying $27.39 for every $1 of expected earnings. That's a premium to the sector's 22.87, but it's below Microsoft's own 5-year average of 30.50.

Growth is what makes the premium defensible. Analysts expect EPS growth of 19.80% in 2028, which is solid for a company already this large. While value investors can find cheaper tech multiples, Microsoft's deep enterprise integration and Copilot expansion firmly position it among the 11 Best Agentic AI Stocks to Buy Right Now . The discount to its own history suggests the market is already pricing in some of the capex risk. That's a reasonable place for the stock to sit heading into the next report.

Big-money sentiment has cooled slightly, with 273 hedge funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, down from 282 in the prior one. Short interest is just 0.82% of the float, pointing to relatively limited bearish positioning.

Azure Has to Keep Earning It

The evidence points to a cloud business with growing contracted demand and steady margins, priced below Microsoft's own historical norm. For long-term investors comfortable with heavy spending in exchange for cloud and AI exposure, the setup looks reasonable. What would change that picture is a sharp slowdown from Azure's 43% pace while capital spending keeps rising. If that happens, today's multiple would start to look a lot less forgiving.

While we acknowledge the potential of MSFT as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Amazon (AMZN) Has a $25B Chip Business. Is the Cash Burn Worth It?
news.Content:
Most people think of Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ) as the place their packages come from. The part of the company drawing the most attention right now sells something far less visible: custom AI chips. In the second quarter of 2026, Amazon Web Services (AWS) said its chips business and its AI business had each passed a $25 billion annual revenue run rate, and both were growing at triple-digit rates.

AWS is Amazon's cloud arm. It rents computing power, storage, and software tools to businesses and charges for what they use. Its homegrown Trainium chips give customers a way to train and run AI models on Amazon's own hardware rather than someone else's. The catch is the bill. Amazon is pouring so much into data centers that free cash flow has turned negative, though that aggressive growth spend is precisely why it remains a core holding among the 10 Best Growth Stocks to Buy Now According to Billionaires . Whether that's a smart bet or an overreach comes down to one thing: how much of the new capacity is already spoken for.

The Customers Say a Lot

The best evidence for Trainium's pull is who's signing up. Anthropic and OpenAI have both made multi-year, multi-gigawatt commitments to the chip, according to Amazon, and companies such as Uber and Pinterest have adopted it too. Deals measured in gigawatts tie a customer's AI plans to Amazon's hardware for years.

Amazon has done this before. Graviton, its general-purpose processor, is used by 98% of the top 1,000 customers of EC2, and revenue commitments for Graviton rose nearly 3x from the prior quarter. Owning the silicon lets AWS control its costs and supply while driving higher margins, a core reason Amazon remains a top holding among the 10 Best Cloud Computing Stocks to Buy According to Billionaires .

AWS Found Another Gear

The chip story shows up in the headline numbers. AWS sales grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, which CEO Andy Jassy described as the unit's fastest growth in 18 quarters. AWS now runs at a $169 billion annualized revenue rate.

AWS operating income reached $16.6 billion, up from $10.2 billion a year earlier, good for a 39.4% margin, while customers spent more on Amazon Bedrock than in all prior quarters combined. Advertising provided a powerful second engine, climbing 26% to $19.8 billion. That combination of high-margin cloud services, expanding ad real estate, and massive AI alliances keeps Amazon anchored among the 10 Stocks With New Strategic Partnerships Investors Should Watch .

Can Amazon Keep Spending Like This?

Story Continues

The objection comes straight from Amazon's own numbers. Purchases of property and equipment hit $54.2 billion in the second quarter, up from $32.2 billion a year earlier. Over the trailing 12 months, free cash flow was an outflow of $7.6 billion, versus an inflow of $18.2 billion the year before, and Amazon tied that swing mainly to AI investment.

That's a real cost. If you own the stock, every new gigawatt of capacity has to find a paying customer. Still, trailing operating cash flow rose 33% to $161.4 billion. The cash drain is a spending choice, not a sign of a weakening core, but it leaves little cushion if AI demand cools, even as major growth investors continue to count it among the 10 Best AI Stocks to Buy According to Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller .

Cheap Next to Its Past, Not Its Peers

At 31.24 times forward earnings, as of October 12, Amazon looks far cheaper than its own history, with a five-year average P/E of 158.85. That long-run figure comes from years when Amazon reinvested nearly everything and reported thin profits, so the gap mostly says the company now earns real money. Next to the sector P/E of 14.80, though, investors are clearly paying a premium for Amazon's growth.

Then there's the wrinkle: expected EPS growth of (18.33)% in 2027. Part of the explanation sits in the second quarter itself. Net income of $62.6 billion, or $5.75 per diluted share, included $53.4 billion of non-operating gains, primarily from Amazon's investments in Anthropic. Earnings lifted by investment gains make a tough comparison for the following year. That's why operating income of $27.5 billion, up 43%, is the cleaner read on the business and the one this analysis leans on.

Even with that context, paying more than 30 times earnings for a profit line expected to shrink only works if AWS keeps compounding. That high-multiple setup is the same bet investors are making across the Top 10 AI Stocks That Will Skyrocket , where market expectations demand relentless top-line cloud growth to justify current valuations. Hedge fund interest ticked up, with 369 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 353 in the prior one. Short interest sits at just 0.88% of the float, which points to relatively limited bearish positioning.

Trainium Holds the Answer

The evidence points to a business whose most important engine is speeding up, not stalling. AWS growth of 37%, a 39.4% margin, and gigawatt-scale chip commitments from two leading AI labs suggest the spending is chasing real demand. The price shows up in negative free cash flow and an EPS forecast that looks gloomy against a base inflated by investment gains.

The setup suits patient growth investors who are comfortable owning a capital-heavy AI build-out at a premium to the sector. If AWS growth slips back while capital spending keeps climbing, that premium gets much harder to defend.

While we acknowledge the potential of AMZN as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Content:

news.Title: GlobalFoundries Eyes $21B Japan-Backed New York Fab Expansion
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in GlobalFoundries Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

GlobalFoundries plans a potential $21 billion, two-phase expansion at its Malta, New York campus, backed and owned through a U.S.-Japan government special-purpose vehicle. The first fab could break ground this quarter, be equipment-ready in 2028 and produce wafers in 2029, pending final agreements.

The two fabs are expected to add roughly 1.8 million wafers of annual capacity, increase U.S. wafer capacity by about 10% and create approximately 27,000 construction and ecosystem jobs plus more than 1,000 manufacturing roles.

GlobalFoundries projects significant financial benefits from technology, construction and operating fees, including about $3 billion in cumulative free cash flow over the next decade and long-term EPS accretion of $0.50 to $0.75. Separately, it will repurpose $955 million in CHIPS funding and give the U.S. Commerce Department an approximately 4% equity stake.

Micron's $250 Billion Bet Could Reshape the AI Memory Race

GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS) said it has been selected to provide technology and operate two new 300-millimeter semiconductor fabs planned for its Malta, New York campus, under an investment framework of up to $21 billion funded by Japan through the U.S.-Japan trade agreement.

Chief Executive Officer Tim Breen called the initiative "one of the most consequential announcements" in the company's history. Under the proposed structure, GlobalFoundries would provide differentiated manufacturing technologies, manage fab construction and operate the facilities, while a dedicated special-purpose vehicle owned by the U.S. and Japanese governments would fund and own the fab infrastructure and tooling.

Quantum Computing's Commercial Breakout Has Arrived

The project remains subject to definitive agreements. The financial figures discussed by the company apply to the first fab only, Chief Financial Officer Sam Franklin said.

Two-Phase Malta Expansion

The program is designed in two phases on land adjacent to GlobalFoundries' existing Fab 8 facility. Each phase is expected to add about 900,000 300-millimeter-equivalent wafers of annual capacity once fully operational.

Quantum Stocks Just Got a Lifeline—Who Benefits Most?

The first phase is shovel-ready, according to Breen, with permitting, environmental approvals and core infrastructure in place. The company said it has lined up key suppliers and has begun early site-enablement work. It expects to break ground during the current quarter, have the fab ready for equipment in 2028 and produce first wafers in 2029.

Story Continues

A decision on whether to proceed with the second fab is expected before the end of 2028. The project is expected to have a minimum term of 20 years.

→ Broadcom's Anthropic Bet Gets Bigger as $60 Billion Financing Raises the Stakes

The new facilities are expected to produce chips based on GlobalFoundries' FDX, BCD and UX platforms. Breen said FDX serves edge and physical AI computing uses, BCD addresses power-management needs including those associated with AI data centers, and UX supports industrial and connected-infrastructure applications. The company may add other technologies over time depending on market conditions and customer requirements.

Domestic Capacity and Economic Impact

Breen said the two fabs are expected to increase total U.S. wafer capacity by roughly 10%, potentially making Malta one of the country's largest semiconductor clusters. GlobalFoundries expects the initiative to create about 27,000 construction and ecosystem jobs, along with more than 1,000 high-skilled manufacturing positions in New York's Capital Region.

The company said the project is intended to reduce reliance on geographically concentrated overseas semiconductor supply for the U.S., while offering Japanese companies access to U.S.-based capacity and reducing geographic concentration and trade exposure.

GlobalFoundries cited its operating history in Malta and a 2023 Singapore brownfield expansion, which it said was completed ahead of plan and on budget, as evidence of its ability to execute large-scale fab projects.

Fee Model and Expected Financial Benefits

Franklin said the government-owned special-purpose vehicle would cover project development, construction, ramp operations, technology and management-fee requirements. GlobalFoundries would receive technology fees, construction-management fees, operating-management fees, reimbursements for allocated shared services and infrastructure, and a share of future EBITDA generated by the vehicle.

Technology fees are expected to begin in 2027 and continue for at least 20 years. Construction-management fees would be earned during the build-out period, while operating-management fees would begin as the first fab comes online around 2029 and rise as production ramps.

Upon final closing of the agreements, GlobalFoundries expects approximately $50 million in revenue contribution in 2027. The company projected annual gross-margin accretion of 30 to 50 basis points in 2027, increasing to 100 to 200 basis points over the long term. It expects operating-margin accretion of 100 to 200 basis points in 2027 and 200 to 300 basis points over the longer term.

GlobalFoundries also forecast earnings-per-share accretion of $0.10 to $0.15 in 2027, growing to $0.50 to $0.75 over the long term, along with approximately $3 billion in cumulative free cash flow from technology and fab-management services over the next decade.

CHIPS Funding and Government Equity Stake

Separately, Breen said the U.S. Department of Commerce CHIPS Program Office has agreed to repurpose $955 million of previously awarded CHIPS funding toward research and development and capital expenditures beginning in 2027. Those investments are intended to support work in silicon germanium, silicon photonics and interposer technologies for AI data centers.

The Department of Commerce will also receive an equity stake in GlobalFoundries of approximately 4%, Breen said. He added that the company does not expect further U.S. government equity participation beyond the announced arrangement.

About GlobalFoundries (NASDAQ:GFS)

GlobalFoundries Inc is a semiconductor contract manufacturer that produces chips for customers without owning their own fabrication facilities. The company operates as a pure-play foundry, manufacturing semiconductors based on customers' designs and supporting them through process development, wafer fabrication, packaging, and related services.

Its technology portfolio focuses on specialized semiconductor platforms rather than the most advanced leading-edge logic nodes. Products and services include radio-frequency technologies, analog and mixed-signal solutions, power management, embedded memory, silicon photonics, and automotive and industrial semiconductor platforms.

news.Title: Amazon’s $550 tablet breaks its oldest hardware rule
news.Content: For years, Amazon made it simple for customers to purchase a Fire tablet: It was inexpensive. Amazon (AMZN) was able to avoid direct comparisons with Apple's iPad and other high-end tablets because of this pricing advantage. However, Amazon is giving up on the selling feature that characterized a large portion of its tablet business with its new Alexa tablet series priced at $549.99. Amazon released three Alexa-branded tablets running Google's Android operating system. They range in price from $229.99 to $549.99. Additionally, the devices have the full Google Play Store and revolve the experience around Amazon's Alexa+ AI assistant. The consumer equation is altered by this change. Apple's entry-level iPad is now more affordable than Amazon's most expensive new tablet, which means consumers can no longer justify their purchase based solely on price. Amazon believes Alexa+ can take the place of that previous benefit. Amazon is leaving the bargain tablet behind The Alexa Tablet 8 is priced at $229.99, while the Alexa Tablet 11 is priced at $329.99. The starting price of the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro is $499.99 (or $549.99 for the anti-glare Nanomatte finish). Additionally, Amazon is improving the hardware with stronger CPUs, better screens, and aluminum bodies. However, software could be the most significant practical difference. Due to Fire tablets' previous reliance on Amazon's App Store, certain well-known Android applications were not easily accessible. The Google Play Store is fully integrated into the new Alexa tablets, providing customers with easy access to services including YouTube, Gmail, Netflix, and Google Docs. This eliminates one of the main drawbacks of the Fire tablet. It also facilitates direct comparisons between Amazon's latest devices and tablets from Apple and Samsung. The regular iPad from Apple is currently available for $449. That means Amazon's $499.99 Alexa Tablet 12 Pro starts above Apple's cheapest iPad, while the $549.99 Nanomatte model lands at essentially the same price as Apple's 256GB iPad. The question rapidly shifts for customers. For the simple reason that it was far less expensive, a cheap Fire tablet may prevail. When a product costs $500 or more, Amazon must justify why it is a better option than an iPad. Alexa+ has to justify the higher price Alexa+ is Amazon's response. Instead of treating the generative AI helper as separate software, the firm integrated it right into the new tablets. Without constantly using the Alexa wake word, users may operate smart home devices, ask questions about information that's currently on the screen, and carry on conversations. Story Continues Amazon used the example of a person looking through hiking routes and asking Alexa which path would be best for them. Without switching applications, a person reading a recipe might ask the assistant to get items. Behind the new lineup, it is the bigger wager. Amazon is substituting an AI edge for its previous pricing advantage. More Amazon: Amazon is coming for your quick Walmart run Amazon's Alexa shopping tool faces its first big October test Amazon pulls a best-selling pain reliever again, and customers need to check their medicine cabinets The Prime subscription comes with Alexa+. According to Reuters , the monthly fee of solo access is $20. Households who already pay for Prime and use Alexa for entertainment, shopping, and smart home management may find the tactic especially effective. However, the timing increases the danger. Reuters reported that Amazon's worldwide tablet market share fell to 1.9% in the second quarter of 2026 from 8% a year earlier. Amazon is therefore asking consumers to pay more for its tablets, even as its market position has weakened. That makes Alexa+ much more than a bonus feature. It has to give shoppers a reason to view Amazon hardware differently. What Amazon investors should watch next Which model customers actually purchase will be the most obvious test. If the majority of consumers choose the $229.99 Alexa Tablet 8, Amazon could have created a superior Fire tablet replacement without sacrificing its standing as a low-cost hardware manufacturer. Amazon will have shown something more significant if customers purchase the $499.99 and $549.99 models: Alexa+ can help push its hardware into the premium market. This development is significant because Amazon can operate independently without the tablet industry. Prime, commerce, entertainment, and the company's larger smart-home ecosystem may all benefit from a successful Alexa device. Amazon's tablet pitch was straightforward for years: pay less than you would on an iPad. That argument disappears at $549.99. It must now be replaced with Alexa+. news.Title: What ETFs Are Buying and Selling: New GuruFocus Page Tracks Daily ETF Flows
news.Content: This article first appeared on GuruFocus . ETFs now hold a large and growing share of the U.S. stock market, so what they buy and sell moves real money. Yet that activity is spread across hundreds of funds and thousands of daily holdings files, and it is hard to see in one place. The new page, What ETFs Are Buying and Selling , pulls it together. It shows which stocks ETFs are net buying and net selling, where ETF money is going by sector, and which names are the most actively traded and most widely held across funds. One chart from the page, Top Stocks by ETF Flow, now also appears on the GuruFocus homepage. What the page shows Is AAPL fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator. A period selector at the top ( 1W, 2W, 1M or 3M ) sets the window for every section below it, so you can compare a week of activity with a quarter. Top 10 Stocks by Net ETF Flow. Two ranked lists side by side. Net Buy shows the stocks with the largest net ETF inflow over the period, and Net Sell shows the largest net outflow. Below them, daily charts plot the net ETF flow into the top names day by day against their share prices, so you can see whether fund buying arrived before, during or after a price move. Over the two weeks, ETF buying went mostly to the largest U.S. stocks, with Apple, Exxon Mobil and Nvidia each drawing more than $3 billion. Net selling was far smaller and led by Taiwan Semiconductor at $216 million. Sector Rankings. Where ETF money went by sector, measured two ways. Net Dollar Flow is dollars bought minus dollars sold. Net Buyers is the number of ETFs that bought minus the number that sold, with each fund counted once however many days it traded. Together they show whether a sector's flow came from many funds or a few large ones. Sector Flow Over Time. Daily net ETF flow for each sector, each plotted against the S&P 500, to show rotations into and out of sectors as the market moves. Every sector drew net ETF buying over the two weeks, but most of it came on one day. Oct. 2 brought about $70 billion, roughly two-thirds of the $102 billion total. Latest Hot Picks. news.Title: Elon Musk's SpaceX Just Announced Good (and Bad) News to Apple Shareholders
news.Content:
Elon Musk has spent his career challenging established industries, from payments to automobiles to space exploration. His latest ambitions could create unexpected tailwinds and headwinds for one of the world's most valuable companies: Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL).

Last week, Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), better known as SpaceX, announced plans to acquire nationwide wireless spectrum, bringing its Starlink satellite business closer to competing with Verizon , AT&T , and T-Mobile .

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

At first glance, that sounds like bad news for telecommunications companies , not for Apple. However, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan identified three ways Starlink could threaten the iPhone maker's business. While I see Mohan's points, there's a way Starlink may benefit Apple in the near term.

SpaceX wants to disrupt the wireless industry

Most Americans buy cellular service through Verizon, AT&T, or T-Mobile. These companies operate networks that connect smartphones through ground-based cell towers. SpaceX wants to challenge that business model.

The company's Starlink Mobile initiative aims to combine satellite connectivity with traditional wireless infrastructure, allowing consumers to receive cellular service across a larger geographic area. To support this vision, SpaceX plans to acquire approximately $8 billion worth of low-frequency wireless spectrum.

Wireless companies need access to frequencies to transmit calls, messages, and internet data. The frequencies SpaceX is acquiring are attractive because they cover long distances and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. When combined with Starlink's satellite network, they could help SpaceX develop an alternative to incumbent wireless carriers.

This is a big deal because SpaceX won't necessarily need to replicate every aspect of traditional cellular infrastructure. But building a reliable nationwide network requires substantial capital expenditures, regulatory approvals, technical execution, and customer adoption.

How does Starlink threaten Apple?

To understand the risk to Apple, investors need to consider how Americans buy smartphones. Rather than charging the full price for a new phone upfront, a wireless carrier usually offers a promotional credit if you trade in your existing device and agree to remain on its network. Essentially, you pay the difference for the new phone, and the promotional credit is typically distributed across your monthly bills. Interestingly, Apple still receives the phone's true selling price. Wireless providers absorb the promotional subsidy because retaining a paying subscriber can be financially worthwhile in the long run.

Story Continues

Bank of America estimates that 53 million iPhones are sold annually across America's three largest wireless carriers, with an average promotional credit of $800 per device. If SpaceX offers cheaper wireless plans without similar smartphone promotions, customers might become less eager to upgrade their iPhones. Mohan estimates that if Starlink captures 10% of the major carriers' postpaid subscriber base, Apple could lose 5 million iPhone sales per year, representing an estimated $6 billion in annual revenue.

In addition, SpaceX could eventually introduce its own lower-cost smartphone. By doing so, Musk would compete with the iPhone directly. These devices could integrate Starlink connectivity with Grok artificial intelligence (AI), creating an ecosystem that rivals Apple's hardware, software, and services businesses.

How Starlink might actually help Apple (for now)

It's important to understand that Starlink has not yet built enough commercial products to erode the dominance of America's largest wireless carriers. Building that business will take years, and increased competition might initially benefit Apple.

If Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile become concerned about losing subscribers to Starlink, they will likely respond by offering more aggressive iPhone promotions. That could encourage consumers to upgrade their devices, potentially supporting Apple's near-term sales.

Furthermore, Starlink's mobile service is designed to work with existing smartphones. This means consumers wouldn't necessarily need to abandon their iPhones to switch providers. Apple also has substantial competitive advantages, including its global installed device base, brand loyalty, and sticky services business.

Investors shouldn't equate Apple's revenue with its profitability. Even if the company eventually loses iPhone sales, that wouldn't automatically translate into an equivalent reduction in earnings. The bigger concern is whether reducing carrier subsidies weakens Apple's pricing power over time.

If investors begin questioning the durability of iPhone demand, they might become less willing to pay a premium multiple for Apple stock. Nevertheless, Mohan maintains a buy rating on Apple stock -- meaning he doesn't think these risks are a reason to abandon the company.

For now, SpaceX's disruption to Apple remains speculative and could take years to materialize, if it does. For existing Apple shareholders, I do not see a compelling reason to sell the stock solely because of Musk's ambitions to enter the communications industry. The more prudent approach is to hold and monitor whether Starlink begins to meaningfully disrupt the wireless sector.

We just issued 'double down' alerts on 3 stocks — find out if Apple made our list

Ever feel like you missed the boat in buying the most successful stocks? Then you'll want to hear this.

On rare occasions, our expert team of analysts issues a "Double Down" stock recommendation for companies that they think are about to pop. If you're worried you've already missed your chance to invest, now is the best time to buy before it's too late. And the numbers speak for themselves:

Apple: if you invested $1,000 when we doubled down in 2008, you'd have $65,100 !*

Netflix: if you invested $1,000 when we doubled down in 2004, you'd have $379,986 !*

Right now, we're issuing "Double Down" alerts for three incredible companies, available when you join Stock Advisor , and there may not be another chance like this anytime soon.

news.Title: Intel CEO says ‘good enough’ Chinese models are winning on price
news.Content:
If you have asked Airbnb's help bot to sort out a booking, part of the answer may have come from a Chinese model. Airbnb Inc. (ABNB) CEO Brian Chesky told Bloomberg in October 2025 that his company relies heavily on Qwen. The model, built by Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. (BABA), is "fast and cheap," he said, as Fortune reported .

Intel Corp. (INTC) CEO Lip-Bu Tan just explained why choices like that are spreading. At a panel hosted by lender DBS in Singapore on Monday, October 12, 2026, he called Chinese models like DeepSeek, Kimi and GLM "good enough." They cost less per token and are being adopted quickly, he said, according to Reuters .

Tan also said quantum computing could become mainstream within three to five years. That is a strikingly short window for a technology many investors still file under someday .

Read together, the remarks sound less like a CEO praising rivals and more like one describing his market. Cheaper models spread AI work across more hardware, and much of it lands on processors Intel sells.

Also read: Elon Musk just handed Intel a new problem Wall Street can't ignore

Cheap tokens create more work for Intel's chips

Lower prices rarely shrink demand for computing. When each answer from a model costs less, companies build AI into more products, and total usage climbs. Tan made a similar point in July, saying AI is driving "unprecedented demand for compute."

Intel's latest results show that pull. Data center and AI revenue jumped 59% to $6.3 billion in the second quarter, according to Intel's earnings release . The release highlighted Xeon systems built for inference and agentic workloads, the everyday running of AI rather than training it.

AI agents push that further. Each agent coordinates tasks, moves data and calls tools, much of it on CPUs rather than GPUs. Low-cost open models make agents cheaper to deploy, which multiplies that background work.

China is Intel's customer, and Washington DC its owner

The China angle cuts both ways. China generated about $12.7 billion of Intel's $52.9 billion in 2025 revenue, based on billing location, according to its annual report . That is nearly a quarter of sales, tied to the same market whose models Tan praised.

Server processors also largely sit outside U.S. export curbs on advanced AI chips. Chinese buyers have been signing longer purchase agreements for them as prices climb. Cheap domestic models running on available server chips create a setup that plays to Intel's strengths.

However, the politics are delicate. The U.S. government took a 9.9% stake in Intel for $8.9 billion in August 2025, according to Intel . Two weeks earlier, President Donald Trump called Tan "highly conflicted" over his China ties, Al Jazeera reported .

Story Continues

Public praise for Chinese AI from that CEO will not go unnoticed in Washington. Investors should treat it as a political risk worth tracking, not a footnote.

Tan's quantum clock runs far faster than Nvidia's

The quantum remark deserves more attention than it got. In January 2025, Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang said that very useful quantum computers were likely 15 to 30 years away, CNBC reported . Quantum stocks plunged, and Huang later softened his view .

Intel's own program offers few public clues. Its latest disclosed quantum chip, Tunnel Falls, dates to 2023, according to Network World . Still, its venture arm, Intel Capital, joined a $178 million funding round for QuantWare, a quantum processor startup, in May 2026.

That makes Tan's short timeline look more like a bet on software than on Intel's hardware. He tied quantum's progress to software that uses infrastructure more efficiently, the same logic behind his support for open models.

More Intel:

Top analyst sets outrageous Intel stock target ahead of earnings

Intel stock jumps as SK Hynix weighs U.S. memory-chip deal

Intel stock surges 9% as surprising turnaround takes shape

Wall Street sees the demand but splits on value

Analysts lean positive but cautious. Intel carries a consensus Buy rating from 49 analysts with an average price target of $118.05, according to StockAnalysis . Still, 32 of those analysts rate the stock Hold.

As of Monday, the shares traded roughly 29% below their 52-week high of $142.35, per StockAnalysis, after climbing from a low of $32.89. That gap suggests investors want proof that hot demand turns into durable profit.

The latest calls show caution:

Hold, $115 target: Susquehanna's Christopher Rolland, Monday, October 12, 2026.

Buy rating maintained: Bank of America's Vivek Arya, Monday, October 12, 2026.

Hold, $114 target: Mizuho's Vijay Rakesh, Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

Hold, $110 target: Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon, Monday, September 21, 2026.

The bull case is that cheaper models carry AI into more apps, often through models users have never heard of. Each new deployment adds demand for processors Intel is racing to supply. The bear case is that Intel's China exposure becomes a political liability while rivals chase the same CPU demand.

AI's next phase may be decided less by who builds the smartest model than by who runs millions of adequate ones cheaply. Tan is betting Intel sells the hardware for that phase.

news.Content:

Alphabet, the Google parent and cloud-services group ( NASDAQ:GOOGL ), launched Gemini 4 Argon to developers, businesses and paid subscribers, while its Class A shares traded at $353.10, down approximately 0.20%, at 10.20 am EST on October 14. The investor question is straightforward: how much paying demand can Google build before its introductory API rates expire on November 30? Broad access gives the model a large potential audience. Turning that reach into repeat spending is the next hurdle.

Google's launch announcement puts introductory API pricing at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. After November 30, those rates double to $4 and $20. Pro and Ultra subscribers get access in the Gemini app and Search's AI Mode, while Ultra subscribers can also use it in Antigravity. That gives Google several routes to customers, but availability alone does not establish the rollout's revenue contribution.

Will customers keep spending when the discount disappears? The valuation chart adds pressure: the $353.10 share price sits 36.97% above the $257.79 GF Value estimate, suggesting investors already price in substantial growth. Argon's commercial test is whether trial usage becomes durable paid demandand whether that demand translates into meaningful earnings.

news.Title: 3 Reasons to Buy Intel Stock Before 2027
news.Content:
Shares of Intel (NASDAQ: INTC) are up about 180% over the past year, as of Oct. 12, reflecting growing demand for its chips for artificial intelligence (AI) workloads.

The stock is more expensive than it was a year ago, but the prospect of sustainable revenue growth from AI leaves room for further gains over the next several years. "AI is driving unprecedented demand for compute, and as we continue to execute, Intel is well-positioned to capture sustainable growth across our CPU franchise, ASICs, advanced packaging, and vast wafer foundry network," CEO Lip-Bu Tan stated in the 2026 second-quarter earnings report.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Here are three reasons the stock is a buy heading into 2027.

1. Strong execution is producing momentum in financial results

Intel has topped its own financial expectations for seven straight quarters. Beating guidance repeatedly shows the company is executing well against its goals and managing its factories and costs, which can support a higher stock price over time as investors gain confidence. Here are the key highlights from the Q2 earnings report that point to building momentum in the business:

Revenue rose 25% year over year to $16.1 billion -- the company's strongest growth in more than 15 years.

Non-GAAP gross margin (the share of revenue left after production costs) reached 41.8%, more than 12 points higher than a year earlier.

Adjusted earnings per share of $0.42 more than doubled the guidance of $0.20, and reversed a loss of $0.10 in the year-ago quarter.

Higher revenue, better manufacturing yields (more working chips per wafer), and stronger average selling prices drove the strong results, with data-center and AI sales growing 59% to $6.3 billion. AI-related businesses made up roughly 70% of Intel's total revenue in the quarter.

CFO David Zinsner said the near-term goal was to get gross margins "comfortably into the 40s" every quarter -- implying the potential for more gains over its Q2 gross margin. Overall, the prospect of expanding margins is a positive for the stock heading into 2027.

2. AI is driving more demand for Intel's processors than it can supply

AI will need a massive number of central processing units (CPUs), as well as specialized accelerators and graphics processing units (GPUs) . CPUs have proven more effective at handling orchestration, data movement, and storage around AI training and inference. The growing use of AI agents (software that performs tasks autonomously) will put more strain on existing compute capacity and is a long-term tailwind for Intel.

Story Continues

Intel faces growing competition in the CPU market from Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia . But all these companies should continue to post robust growth, since demand for CPUs continues to outrun supply.

AI agents require a four to six times increase in CPU requirements, which is leading to higher core counts and more stable pricing. Beyond servers, Intel sees further opportunities in edge computing and physical AI systems such as industrial equipment and robotics.

These opportunities support analysts' expectations that Intel's revenue will increase by 21% in 2027, reaching $78 billion.

3. Manufacturing progress is opening additional growth opportunities

Intel's foundry efforts (making chips for other companies) and advanced packaging technology, which connects multiple chips into more powerful processing systems, are showing progress. The 18A process is in high-volume production. Better yields and execution in ramping new technologies mean Intel can produce more chips at lower cost, which improves margins and can attract outside customers for Intel's foundry.

Management sees its advanced packaging business potentially reaching billions of dollars in revenue with attractive margins. Revenue is expected to ramp more meaningfully in the second half of 2027 and can also open the door to larger foundry deals.

Intel's foundry posted a Q2 operating loss of $2.1 billion, although the loss narrowed by $348 million over Q1. The foundry's persistent losses have been an overhang on the stock in recent years, but management is working to bring this business to breakeven by the end of 2027 or into 2028. Narrowing losses at Intel Foundry could support a higher stock price in 2027.

Intel's shares are not cheap, trading at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 67 on 2026 earnings estimates. Even so, accelerating growth, expanding margins, and long-term opportunities in physical AI could still support excellent returns for investors in 2027 and beyond. The forward multiple drops to 49 on 2027 estimates, with analysts expecting 69% annualized earnings growth in the next several years.

news.Title: Cathie Wood buys $17.3 million of surging AI stock
news.Content:
Cathie Wood, chief of Ark Investment Management, often makes bold moves in tech stocks, sometimes reversing course shortly after a trade.

That's what she just did with Meta Platforms (META), buying shares of the social media giant just days after selling them. Meta stock has surged about 17% over the past month.

Last year, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. So far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is up 13.33% as of writing, while the S&P 500 surged 14.02 %, Yahoo Finance data shows.

Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a rosy 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the ETF tumbled more than 60%.

Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of Oct. 13, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -4.97% , while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 12.33% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar .

Cathie Wood remains optimistic about AI and tech revolution

Wood focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, but their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds.

Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to a report by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott . That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking.

Wood defended her investment strategy after an audience member at a recent summit questioned ARK's performance compared with the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ).

"I welcome the question. Investors deserve to understand both their returns and the decisions behind them," Wood wrote in an Oct. 5 post on X .

Related: Cathie Wood sells $15.8 million of popular semiconductor stock

She argued that the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and QQQ are built differently. QQQ tracks the Nasdaq-100 Index, while ARK actively invests in companies it believes are driving disruptive innovation across industries including healthcare, financial services, and transportation.

Wood has long been optimistic about AI, which she sees as a major driver of productivity, economic growth, and corporate profits in the years ahead. She has also pushed back against recent fears that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity.

On Sept. 12, Wood reposted a post by David Sacks on X , saying he makes a good case that the "AI will kill humanity" headlines were orchestrated.

Story Continues

Meanwhile, Wood acknowledged that AI, like other technologies, can be used for harmful purposes. She said people such as Elon Musk, who highlight AI's potential risks, are "doing us a great service," adding that "half of the solution — including AI — is understanding the problem."

In August, Wood said U.S. corporate profits remain unusually strong, with domestic profits before tax at 13.2% of GDP, a level she said is near multi-decade highs.

Some of that strength came from the massive monetary and fiscal stimulus during the pandemic, but Wood believes another factor is helping sustain margins today: Companies are leaning into AI and productivity gains to protect them.

"I think we're still early in seeing how far that can go," she said, adding that companies using AI effectively will "separate themselves from the ones that don't."

Not all investors agree with Wood's optimism. Over the past 12 months through Oct. 12, the Ark Innovation ETF saw roughly $1.6 billion in net outflows, according to data from ETF research firm VettaFi .

Cathie Wood buys $17.3 million of Meta stock

On Oct. 13, Wood's Ark funds bought a total of 22,734 shares of Meta Platforms (META), according to Ark's daily trading information sent to TheStreet. These shares were worth about $17.3 million based on the latest trading price of $762.5.

That was a quick reversal of her recent selling of 24,299 shares on Oct. 8 and 12.

The social media giant is pushing deeper into AI agents. In September, it launched Muse, a personal AI agent that can take actions on users' behalf and help with daily tasks such as sending emails.

The app has now become one of the most popular personal AI agents since its debut, climbing to the top of Apple's App Store ahead of ChatGPT.

Related: Cathie Wood buys $3.5 million of surging tech stock

After rolling out Muse, Meta is also working with companies like Walmart and Stripe to bring AI agents further into the business world. Those companies are developing a "personal agent protocol," an open standard that defines how AI agents interact with businesses, CNBC reported . Still, Amazon (AMZN) has blocked Meta's agents over concerns about website scraping.

Shares of Meta have gained roughly 17% over the past month. Year to date, shares are up 15%.

Perhaps the next catalyst for Meta stock is its third-quarter earnings results, which will be released on Oct. 21.

In July, Meta posted earnings of $6.18 per share, missing analysts' expectations of $7.22, while revenue of $60.80 billion topped estimates of $60.17 billion. Shares fell afterward as the company also issued weaker-than-expected revenue guidance.

Truist analyst Youssef Squali raised the firm's price target on Meta Platforms (META) to $1,000 from $763 and maintained a Buy rating on the shares, The Fly reported on Oct. 13.

Squali adjusted the valuation model to FY27 from FY26 to reflect the expected contribution from Muse, offset by higher capital expenditure expectations.

Truist remains "constructive" on Meta stock heading into earnings, expecting results at the higher end of guidance and consensus estimates, driven by strong monetization and user engagement.

Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski also recently raised the firm's price target on Meta Platforms to $1,000 from $796 and kept an Overweight rating on the stock.

The analyst said the enthusiasm around the Muse product cycle was "warranted." However, he expects Meta's third-quarter earnings to offer some caution for investors who are expecting Muse to make a financial contribution in 2027.

The analyst also expects Wall Street's 2027 EPS to likely fall due to higher operating expenses.

Meta is not a top-10 holding in the Ark Innovation ETF.

Top 10 holdings in the Ark Innovation ETF by market value and weight as of Oct. 13, 2026:

Tesla (TSLA) – $639.1 million, 9.79%

SpaceX (SPCX) – $442.6 million, 6.78%

Tempus AI (TEM) – $323.4 million, 4.95%

Other than buying Meta shares, Wood's latest trades included buying Kodiak AI (KDK), Cerebras Systems (CBRS), Beam Therapeutics (BEAM), Freenome (FRNM), Scribe Therapeutics (SCTX), Nurix Therapeutics (NRIX), and Kymera Therapeutics (KYMR).

She also sold shares of Teradyne (TER), DraftKings (DKNG), Everpure (P), Toast (TOST), CareDx (CDNA), Personalis (PSNL), and Alibaba (BABA).

news.Title: Applied Materials vs. Intel: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
news.Content:
When choosing a technology stock, you can weigh a chipmaker against a supplier of the equipment chipmaking requires. Which is the better buy, Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) or Intel (NASDAQ:INTC)?

Applied Materials sells the equipment and services that chipmakers use to fabricate semiconductors, and its fiscal year ends in late October. Intel designs and manufactures its own processors for PCs and data centers, and its fiscal year ends in late December. The two companies sit at different points in the semiconductor supply chain.

The case for Applied Materials

In its annual report for the fiscal year ended Oct. 26, 2025, Applied Materials describes itself as the leader in the materials engineering solutions used to produce virtually every semiconductor in the world.

That filing also shows a concentrated customer base, with two customers accounting for about 19% and 15% of net revenue. Customer concentration like this adds risk. In May 2026, Applied announced a new innovation partnership with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) at its Silicon Valley EPIC Center to develop technologies for AI chips.

On Oct. 6, 2026, Applied also announced a collaboration with Intel, bringing teams together at the EPIC Center and Intel's R&D campus in Hillsboro, Oregon, to work on next-generation transistors and advanced packaging. The announcement gives no financial terms.

In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $28.4 billion, up about 4.4% from the prior year. Net income was close to $7.0 billion, which works out to a net margin of roughly 24.7%, down from 26.4% in fiscal 2024. The dip came from taxes.

Pretax income rose about 14%, but the income tax provision more than doubled to $2.3 billion. The annual report attributes the jump to a $659 million effect from remeasuring deferred tax assets in Singapore and a $407 million valuation allowance on corporate alternative minimum tax credits.

The latest quarter looks stronger than the annual figures. In the quarter ended July 26, 2026, which Applied reported on Aug. 13, revenue rose 25% to $9.1 billion and net income rose 43% to $2.5 billion. The company returned $860 million to shareholders in the quarter through $440 million in share repurchases and $420 million in dividends.

For the fiscal fourth quarter, management guided to revenue of $10.25 billion, plus or minus $500 million.

As of its July 26, 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, calculated from total debt, was approximately 0.3x, based on total debt of $6.5 billion and shareholders' equity of $25.6 billion.

Story Continues

The debt-to-equity ratio compares total debt to shareholders' equity, showing how much debt a company uses to fund its assets. The current ratio, which measures a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations with assets that can be converted into cash within a year, stood at roughly 2.4x on the same date. For fiscal 2025, Applied Materials generated nearly $5.7 billion in free cash flow: $8.0 billion in operating cash flow minus $2.3 billion in capital expenditures.

Free cash flow is the cash a company generates after accounting for the money spent to maintain or expand its physical assets.

The case for Intel

Intel describes itself in its annual report as an integrated device manufacturer, meaning it designs its own chips and predominantly makes them in its own factories.

The company is also working to expand Intel Foundry, which makes chips for other companies. In the second quarter of 2026, Intel Foundry reported $5.8 billion in revenue, up 31%, and an operating loss of $2.1 billion.

In August 2025, the U.S. government agreed to buy 433.3 million Intel shares at $20.47 each, a 9.9% stake costing $8.9 billion, and received a five-year warrant for an additional 5% stake, exercisable only if Intel ceases to own at least 51% of its foundry business. Intel said the government's ownership is passive, with no board representation.

In fiscal 2025, which ended Dec. 27, 2025, revenue was about $52.9 billion, down nearly 0.5% from the previous year. Intel reported a net loss attributable to Intel of $267 million, or a net margin of roughly -0.5%.

The loss was small because interest and other income of $3.3 billion offset a $2.2 billion operating loss, and that line included a $5.3 billion gain from divestitures, including the sale of Altera.

The company remains focused on returning to profitability while managing its large manufacturing footprint.

The second quarter of 2026, which ended June 27, looked very different. Revenue rose 25% to $16.1 billion, operating income was $1.8 billion, and Intel's non-GAAP earnings per share were $0.42.

Intel still reported a GAAP net loss attributable to Intel of $11.0 billion, or $2.16 per share. The cause was a $12.5 billion noncash loss from changes in the fair value of shares held in escrow under the U.S. government agreement, not a deterioration in operations. For the third quarter, Intel guided to revenue of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion and non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.38.

As of June 27, 2026, Intel's debt-to-equity ratio, calculated using total debt of $50.5 billion and Intel stockholders' equity of $87.5 billion, was approximately 0.6x, and its current ratio was approximately 1.6x. At the end of 2025, those figures were about 0.4x and 2.0x.

Equity fell in the first half of 2026 partly because of $13.6 billion of escrowed share losses. In April, Intel reacquired Apollo's 49% stake in its Ireland fab joint venture for $14.2 billion in cash, which Intel said it would fund with cash on hand and about $6.5 billion of new debt.

By my calculation, Intel's 2025 operating cash flow of $9.7 billion fell short of the $14.6 billion it spent on property, plant and equipment, resulting in negative free cash flow of about $4.9 billion on that basis.

Intel's own non-GAAP adjusted free cash flow, which nets out government incentives and partner contributions, was negative $1.6 billion. Stock-based compensation, a noncash expense added back in the cash flow statement, was $2.4 billion, or roughly 25.1% of operating cash flow.

Risk profile comparison

Applied Materials operates in an industry that, according to its annual report, has historically been cyclical and subject to volatility in customer demand. China made up 28% of its revenue in the July 2026 quarter, down from 35% a year earlier, so U.S. export controls and trade policy remain a risk.

In February 2026, Applied agreed to pay $252.5 million to the U.S. Department of Commerce, according to its announcement, to resolve allegations that it reexported chipmaking equipment to Semiconductor Manufacturing International (SMIC) in China without required licenses between November 2020 and July 2022, according to the Bureau of Industry and Security's settlement documents.

The Justice Department and the SEC closed their related investigations without action. Under the settlement, Applied agreed to conduct two annual audits of its export compliance program for 2026 and 2027. The annual report also warns of cybersecurity incidents and of future impairment charges on goodwill or intangible assets.

Intel's turnaround depends on its foundry business, which lost money in the second quarter even as revenue grew.

Its annual report says leading-edge manufacturing requires substantial capital investment and a cost structure that needs manufacturing volumes beyond what Intel expects from its own products. Existing shareholders' ownership stakes have also been diluted.

In August 2026, Intel sold about 242.1 million new shares at $95 each, raising about $23 billion, including the underwriters' option, which they exercised in full; in September 2025, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) agreed to invest $5 billion in Intel stock at $23.28 per share. The government's warrants cover up to 241 million additional shares at $20 each, but they become exercisable only if Intel ceases to own at least 51% of its foundry business.

A shareholder also filed a derivative lawsuit in March 2026 against Intel's directors, the Department of Commerce and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

It alleges the directors breached their fiduciary duties by approving the August 2025 government agreement and seeks to invalidate the deal.

The case moved to federal court in April, defendants filed motions to dismiss in May, and the case remained pending as of Intel's July 2026 quarterly report.

Valuation comparison

Applied Materials has the higher profit margin, while Intel trades at a lower price-to-sales ratio and a higher forward price-to-earnings ratio.

Metric

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The Forward P/E ratio measures the current stock price against future earnings estimates, while the P/S ratio measures market value relative to sales over the past twelve months.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

While Applied Materials looks like the better buy to me, I'd be a patient buyer and add shares over time instead of all at once.

The company sells the equipment chipmakers need as they expand, and its latest quarter showed revenue growing about 25%. Management also said it is raising its revenue expectations for its chip equipment business for calendar 2026. The company keeps turning a large share of its sales into profit and returns cash to shareholders.

The caveat is that chip equipment is a cyclical business. Applied's annual report says its industry has historically been cyclical, and China still accounted for a little more than a quarter of recent revenue, so export controls and the Commerce Department settlement remain in view.

The stock can also be volatile, so spreading purchases out makes sense to me.

Intel is the more difficult case. The second-quarter loss of about $11 billion was due to a noncash accounting charge, so I wouldn't read it as a collapse in the business.

But the foundry unit is still losing money, and factory spending is heavy. The company also sold $23 billion in new stock in August, diluting existing owners.

The shares trade well above the price the U.S. government paid for its stake. If the foundry business starts earning money, Intel deserves a fresh look.

Either one is best owned as part of a diversified portfolio of at least 50 companies that you plan to hold for years.

news.Title: Berkshire Hathaway Quietly Built a $37.4 Billion Stake in Alphabet, Making It the Portfolio's Third-Largest Position
news.Content:
If you've been a longtime fan and follower of Berkshire Hathaway 's (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) former chief stock-picker Warren Buffett, then you know he's steered clear of technology stocks , arguing they're too difficult to understand.

That is, until somewhat recently. Berkshire took on a small (now-exited) position in Amazon back in 2019, and of course, Apple has grown to become the conglomerate's single-biggest equity holding since first stepping into it back in 2016. It's not clear to what extent these were Buffett-directed trades, and to be fair, both companies are as much consumer-oriented as they are technology names, making their businesses at least somewhat easier to understand.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

If there was any doubt that Warren Buffett has officially warmed up to tech stocks, though, it's been wiped away this year by Berkshire's entry into a sizable stake in Google parent Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL).

Big commitment

It wasn't clear to what extent Warren Buffett had a hand in the matter when Berkshire first scooped up 17.8 million A shares of Alphabet in Q3 of 2025. By then, the Oracle of Omaha had already announced his then-impending retirement as CEO at the end of that same year, and seemed more interested in cleaning up some loose ends rather than adding new stocks to the company's portfolio. Besides, it was only about a $5 billion stake at the time, suggesting perhaps that he'd merely allowed one of his lieutenants to take on a token position.

That changed dramatically in the first quarter of this year, however, when Berkshire bought another 36.4 million A shares of Alphabet, and then 24.5 million in Q2. Paired with the 27.2 million C shares of Alphabet purchased this year, this $37.4 billion (combined) holding accounts for a little over 10% of Berkshire Hathaway's $358 billion stock portfolio, making it the conglomerate's third-biggest holding.

The kicker: This was largely Buffett's idea after all. Although he still consults with current CEO Greg Abel on such matters, in an interview with CNBC this July, Warren Buffett plainly explained: "I initiated it."

The sector itself isn't exactly the stumbling block

This still doesn't mean Berkshire is embracing all technology stocks. As Buffett said in the very same interview, "I would say that I don't like it as well as at least four or five other businesses that we own."

Story Continues

It also doesn't mean Buffett is still calling all the shots despite no longer being CEO or chairman of the board . He adds, "I am not doing anything that he [current CEO Greg Abel] doesn't approve of. He's not doing anything I don't approve of. We talk all the time, but he is the decider."

Rather, it's a recognition that at least two major technology companies meet a very specific requirement Buffett looks for in all of Berkshire Hathaway's holdings -- that is, "businesses that are going to earn high returns on capital for an extended period of time."

And that's a simple criterion more investors might want to consider before buying any new stock, in or out of the technology sector. It certainly seems to be working for Berkshire, allowing the conglomerate to buy and hold names it arguably wouldn't have at one point in its history.

news.Title: Can Coherent's AI Data Center Expansion Fuel Long-Term Growth?
news.Content:
Coherent Corp. COHR is strengthening its position in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market through capacity expansion and advanced optical technologies. The company's efforts to increase manufacturing output, improve connectivity performance and develop energy-efficient solutions should help it capitalize on rising demand for high-speed data center infrastructure.

Capacity Expansion Strengthens COHR's AI Growth Prospects

Coherent is accelerating production investments to meet increasing demand for optical components used in AI computing environments. The company aims to double its internal indium phosphide (InP) manufacturing capacity by the end of 2026, followed by another expansion exceeding twofold by 2027.

Its transition toward six-inch wafer manufacturing supports higher production yields than conventional three-inch processes. This manufacturing platform accommodates electro-absorption modulated lasers, continuous-wave lasers and photodiodes, helping Coherent improve production efficiency and address growing customer requirements.

Higher manufacturing capacity should enhance supply availability, strengthen customer relationships and create opportunities to capture additional spending from hyperscale data center operators.

Advanced Optical Technologies Support Competitive Positioning

Beyond manufacturing expansion, Coherent is developing optical networking technologies designed to accommodate increasingly demanding AI workloads. Its portfolio includes silicon photonics, co-packaged optics and vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers, providing customers with multiple connectivity options.

The company's 400G-per-lane technology enables faster information transfer, while its advanced optical transport solutions can quadruple fiber transmission capacity. These capabilities should support increasingly complex AI infrastructure requirements.

Energy Efficiency Adds Another Growth Opportunity

Coherent is also advancing thermal management technologies and optical components that reduce energy consumption during data transmission. Such innovations could become increasingly important as operators seek to manage power requirements and infrastructure expenses.

Although substantial capital investments and manufacturing execution risks remain concerns, expanding production capabilities and technological innovation should strengthen Coherent's competitive standing in the AI infrastructure market.

How Are Coherent's Industry Peers Positioned?

Lumentum Holdings LITE and Applied Optoelectronics AAOI are expanding their presence in the AI optical networking market. Lumentum is investing in advanced laser technologies and manufacturing capacity to address growing hyperscaler requirements. Its strategic collaboration with NVIDIA strengthens opportunities in next-generation optical connectivity. Lumentum's broader photonics portfolio also supports high-bandwidth networking applications.

Story Continues

Meanwhile, Applied Optoelectronics is benefiting from demand for advanced data center transceivers. The company secured significant orders for 800G optical products and is expanding manufacturing capabilities. Applied Optoelectronics is also progressing with 1.6T technology, positioning it to serve increasingly bandwidth-intensive AI infrastructure deployments worldwide.

COHR's Price Performance & Estimates

COHR stock has surged 162.6% over the past year against the industry's 23.3% decline.

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

From a valuation standpoint, COHR trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 27.26X, above the industry's 19.51X. It carries a Value Score of C.

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for COHR's fiscal 2027 earnings increased over the past 60 days.

COHR stock currently carries a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here .

news.Title: Tesla's Roadster event is back on for Thursday night. Here's what to expect.
news.Content:
After a two-week delay, the Tesla ( TSLA ) Roadster event is back on — for now.

This week, Tesla added a countdown clock to its Tesla Roadster website , stating that the reveal would occur at 7:55 p.m. CDT on Oct. 15, two weeks after the initial Oct. 1 reveal date. Tesla said the reveal was pushed back due to weather conditions at the demo site, SpaceX's ( SPCX ) Rocket Development and Testing facility in Waco, Texas . The event will be streamed on Tesla's X account .

Stormy weather would've likely hampered the Roadster's rumored hovering or flying ability. The Information reported several weeks ago that the reveal event on Oct. 1 could include a demonstration of a limited-edition version of the Roadster equipped with cold-gas thrusters developed in collaboration with SpaceX ( SPCX ), possibly including airborne flight.

Tesla is asking prospective buyers to put down a $5,000 deposit, followed by a $45,000 wire transfer due within 10 days of the initial deposit.

Tesla has not said how much the new Roadster will cost, though it is expected to exceed $250,000. However, when Tesla announced the 7:55 p.m. CDT reveal time on X.com, CEO Elon Musk replied, "Timing is everything," suggesting the digits may have some meaning.

Longtime analyst and Tesla bull Pierre Ferragu suggested it could have something to do with the price, then coyly threw out the number $75,990. He later followed up with the idea that the Roadster event should start at "7:59:90." Some have suggested this could refer to the starting price of the car's base model or to a particular track time the Roadster achieved.

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever EV and used a Lotus Elise chassis.

Tesla announced its successor way back in 2017, took in reservations with those high deposits, and originally said deliveries would begin in 2020. Those initial reservation holders have been waiting for quite a long time.

During his appearance on the All-In Summit , Musk brought up the Tesla Roadster.

"It'll be a banger. Excitement guaranteed. Success is not guaranteed, but excitement is," he added, with All-In host Jason Calacanis claiming he had seen a preview of the event, and that the demo would "blow people's minds."

news.Title: Apple retakes $5 trillion market cap, only second company to eclipse milestone number
news.Content: Apple's ( AAPL ) market capitalization once again crossed the $5 trillion mark on Wednesday, just months after it first touched the threshold in late July. It's been just under a year since Apple's market cap topped $4 trillion in October 2025. The company's stock price is up roughly 26% year to date and nearly 40% over the past 12 months. Apple stock climbed more than 1% Wednesday. The milestone comes a little more than a month after John Ternus took over as Apple CEO from Tim Cook , who stepped down on Sept. 1, a day after Apple debuted its HomeView smart home hub amid a renewed effort to grab share in the smart home market. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ) currently dominate that space . Apple has also benefited from strong iPhone sales throughout 2026 on the back of a renewed upgrade cycle. The company has also finally fleshed out its AI strategy after investors heavily criticized the iPhone maker for initially falling behind in the AI race and struggling to catch up. Apple unveiled its Apple Intelligence platform at its WWDC event in 2024, but the company delayed a number of features, leaving Wall Street to question Apple's ability to compete with rivals, including Google and Microsoft ( MSFT ). But the company has since won a reprieve. It has partnered with Google to use some of the search giant's AI models and rolled out a number of major updates to Apple Intelligence, including its Siri AI, though the software is still in beta. And then there's the iPhone Duo foldable, which, at $1,999, could boost the iPhone line's average selling price and the company's bottom line. Apple is also preparing to launch its first touch-screen MacBook and revamped iPads later this month, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman . But Apple is also working to contend with the ongoing memory and storage shortage, which has forced it to raise prices on its iPhones, iPads, and Macs, driving fears that sales could take a hit.
